Both combine changes from one branch into another, but differently:

**Merge** creates a new commit that joins two histories together, preserving both branches exactly as they happened. Nothing is rewritten — you get a merge commit with two parents.

**Rebase** takes your commits and replays them one by one on top of another branch's tip, producing new commits (new hashes) with a linear history. The original commits still exist until garbage collected, but your branch now looks like it was built on top of the latest target branch from the start.

**Trade-offs:**
- Merge preserves true history (what actually happened, including when branches diverged) but can leave a messy commit graph with lots of merge bubbles.
- Rebase gives a clean, linear, easy-to-read history but rewrites commit hashes — which is dangerous on shared/pushed branches since anyone who already pulled the old commits will get conflicts (diverged history).

**When to reach for each:**
- **Rebase** your own local feature branch before opening a PR, to clean up commits and land on a linear history against `main`/`master`. Also good for `git pull --rebase` to avoid pointless merge commits when syncing with upstream.
- **Merge** when integrating a completed feature branch into `main` (especially via PR merge) — it's non-destructive and keeps an accurate record. Also always merge (never rebase) branches other people are actively pulling from.
- Golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed and others may have based work on — rebase local/private history, merge public/shared history.
